#| include: false
#| autorun: true
# Lab machinery: the estimator of the course, the specification menu, its
# validation, and the helpers of Tasks 4 and 5 – try_spec(), my_experiments(),
# submit_exploration(), prereg(), run_spec() and report_result(). The same
# code as R/spec_tools.R of the downloadable workspace, apart from the tag of
# the class chart, which lasts for the browser session here. Every
# specification is fitted live; data/spec_curve.csv places it among the 64,
# and data/menu_options.csv gives the reason for every option that is not on
# the curve. Both arrive with the page through its `resources:` list, in the
# folder that the setup cell of the including page names as .data_dir.

# ============================================================================
# CONFIGURATION – the class chart and the course site
# ============================================================================
# The results Form that submit_exploration() and report_result() pre-fill: its
# ID and the entry codes of its seven fields. They belong to the shared results
# Form of the course; a Form of its own replaces them here and nowhere else.
# The word in .case_word follows the tag in every label, so that the chart of
# this case study reads only its own rows.
.form_id <- "1FAIpQLSezoAEOnZUfP4pkfN28_XtEBwSyc2RLsXB-h8RPSegF7_t76A"
.form_entry <- c(spec = "entry.832496914", b = "entry.1656311800", se = "entry.1337458262",
                 t = "entry.1940779437", df = "entry.1682711955", n = "entry.1586392724",
                 r = "entry.1660273001")
.case_word <- "housing"
.course_url <- "https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-housing"
# ============================================================================


# ---- The estimator -------------------------------------------------------------
# A verbatim copy of R/_tools.R in the course repository, which builds
# the curve; the downloadable workspace carries the same copy in R/spec_tools.R.

# The same code runs in the downloadable workspace and in webR on the browser
# lab, so all three give the same numbers. The standard errors and the average
# marginal effect come from packages: parameters with sandwich for the HC2
# errors of the linear model, marginaleffects for the average marginal effect
# of the logit. R/check_parity.R in the course repository checks both
# against estimatr and margins. The rows are chosen with dplyr, because
# datawizard evaluates its conditions in a fresh environment and so cannot see
# the arguments of a function.

# The options of the curve, in menu order. Anything else is refused by
# check_spec() with the reason recorded in data/menu_options.csv.
SPEC_AXES <- list(
  comparison = c("white", "nonhispanic"),
  population = c("replies", "all"),
  uncoded    = c("drop", "not_named"),
  model      = c("lpm", "logit"),
  adjust     = c("none", "email", "place", "place_ethnic")
)

# Covariates of each adjustment set; all are recorded before the emails went out.
ADJUST_TERMS <- list(
  none         = character(0),
  email        = "hard_email",
  place        = c("hard_email", "pop_third", "poverty_third"),
  place_ethnic = c("hard_email", "pop_third", "poverty_third", "black_third", "hispanic_third")
)

# The analysed rows and the outcome of one specification. Bounced emails never
# reached an official and are outside the experiment under every option.
spec_frame <- function(housing, comparison = "white", population = "replies", uncoded = "drop") {  # r-style: approved
  housing |>
    dplyr::filter(!is.na(reply),
                  .env$comparison == "nonhispanic" | group %in% c("white", "hispanic"),
                  .env$population == "all" | reply == 1) |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      hisp = as.integer(group == "hispanic"),
      y = dplyr::case_when(reply == 0 ~ 0,
                           is.na(named) & .env$uncoded == "not_named" ~ 0,
                           .default = named)
    ) |>
    dplyr::filter(!is.na(y))
}

# The conversion rules of the robustness study (standard_correlation_coefficient.R in
# github.com/marton-balazs-kovacs/multi100): t with its df, which is the rule of
# effectsize::t_to_r(); z with the sample size standing in for the missing df;
# a chi-square read as the square of a z, so it carries no sign.
r_robustness <- function(stat, stat_type, df, n) {  # r-style: approved
  dplyr::case_when(
    stat_type == "t" ~ effectsize::t_to_r(stat, df, ci = NULL)$r,
    stat_type == "z" ~ tanh(abs(stat) * sqrt(1 / (n - 3))) * sign(stat),
    stat_type == "chi2" ~ tanh(sqrt(abs(stat)) * sqrt(1 / (n - 3)))
  )
}

check_spec <- function(comparison, population, uncoded, model, adjust) {  # r-style: approved
  chosen <- list(comparison = comparison, population = population, uncoded = uncoded,
                 model = model, adjust = adjust)
  bad <- names(chosen)[!purrr::map2_lgl(chosen, SPEC_AXES[names(chosen)], \(v, ok) v %in% ok)]
  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    stop("Not on the curve: ", paste0(bad, " = '", unlist(chosen[bad]), "'", collapse = ", "),
         ". The options are listed in data/menu_options.csv.", call. = FALSE)
  }
  invisible(TRUE)
}

# One specification: estimate in percentage points (negative = Hispanic names
# greeted by name less often, the direction of the claim), its SE and 95%
# interval, the test of the model that the specification fits, and the partial
# correlation by the rule of the robustness study.
fit_spec <- function(housing, comparison = "white", population = "replies", uncoded = "drop",  # r-style: approved
                     model = "lpm", adjust = "none") {
  check_spec(comparison, population, uncoded, model, adjust)
  terms <- ADJUST_TERMS[[adjust]]
  # only the model columns, and only the emails with every covariate;
  # marginaleffects refuses a data column called `group`
  frame <- spec_frame(housing, comparison, population, uncoded) |>
    dplyr::select("y", "hisp", dplyr::all_of(terms)) |>
    stats::na.omit()
  form <- stats::reformulate(c("hisp", terms), response = "y")

  if (model == "lpm") {
    fit <- stats::lm(form, data = frame)
    # HC2 errors (MacKinnon and White 1985) from sandwich::vcovHC() (Zeileis
    # 2004, Journal of Statistical Software), with the t test on the residual df
    coefs <- parameters::model_parameters(fit, vcov = "HC2")
    row <- datawizard::data_filter(coefs, Parameter == "hisp")
    test <- list(coef = row$Coefficient, coef_se = row$SE, stat_type = "t", stat = row$t,
                 df = row$df_error, p = row$p)
    est <- list(b = row$Coefficient, se = row$SE, low = row$CI_low, high = row$CI_high)
  } else {
    fit <- stats::glm(form, family = stats::binomial(), data = frame)
    coefs <- parameters::model_parameters(fit, ci_method = "wald")
    row <- datawizard::data_filter(coefs, Parameter == "hisp")
    test <- list(coef = row$Coefficient, coef_se = row$SE, stat_type = "z", stat = row$z,
                 df = NA_real_, p = row$p)
    # The average marginal effect: the mean over the analysed emails of the
    # predicted probability with a Hispanic name minus that with a comparison
    # name, with delta-method errors (marginaleffects; Arel-Bundock, Greifer and
    # Heiss 2024, Journal of Statistical Software)
    ame <- marginaleffects::avg_comparisons(fit, variables = list(hisp = 0:1))
    est <- list(b = ame$estimate, se = ame$std.error, low = ame$conf.low, high = ame$conf.high)
  }

  tibble::tibble(
    comparison = comparison, population = population, uncoded = uncoded,
    model = model, adjust = adjust,
    b_pp = 100 * est$b, se_pp = 100 * est$se,
    coef = test$coef, coef_se = test$coef_se,
    stat_type = test$stat_type, stat = test$stat, df = test$df, p = test$p,
    r = r_robustness(test$stat, test$stat_type, test$df, nrow(frame)),
    n = nrow(frame), n_hisp = sum(frame$hisp == 1), n_comp = sum(frame$hisp == 0),
    rate_hisp = 100 * mean(frame$y[frame$hisp == 1]),
    rate_comp = 100 * mean(frame$y[frame$hisp == 0]),
    ci_low = 100 * est$low, ci_high = 100 * est$high
  )
}

# The free-text label that carries a specification to the class chart.
spec_line <- function(comparison, population, uncoded, model, adjust) {  # r-style: approved
  sprintf("comparison=%s population=%s uncoded=%s model=%s adjust=%s",
          comparison, population, uncoded, model, adjust)
}


# ---- The menu --------------------------------------------------------------------
# The eleven decisions in the order of the menu, each with the options that the
# curve keeps. The five decisions of SPEC_AXES keep two or more options, which
# multiply to the 64 specifications; on the other six the curve keeps one.
# Every other option is a row of data/menu_options.csv, whose reason the
# helpers print when it is asked for.
.menu <- list(
  # The question
  outcome    = "named",
  comparison = SPEC_AXES$comparison,
  population = SPEC_AXES$population,
  names      = "both",
  officials  = "any",
  # Measurement
  uncoded    = SPEC_AXES$uncoded,
  bounced    = "exclude",
  # The model
  model      = SPEC_AXES$model,
  adjust     = SPEC_AXES$adjust,
  inference  = "model",
  scale      = "pp"
)
.level_titles <- c(estimand    = "The question",
                   measurement = "Measurement",
                   estimation  = "The model")


# ---- The shipped files -----------------------------------------------------------
# Each file is read once and cached. The base reader keeps this code identical,
# line for line, with the copy in R/spec_tools.R of the workspace. An empty cell must read as
# NA, as readr reads it: the 14 authorities without community thirds would
# otherwise enter the adjusted models as a fourth level "".
.cache <- new.env(parent = emptyenv())
.read_once <- function(name, path) {  # r-style: approved
  if (is.null(.cache[[name]])) {
    if (!file.exists(path))
      stop(sprintf("%s is missing – the page loads it through its resources list. Reload the page.",
                   path), call. = FALSE)
    assign(name, utils::read.csv(path, stringsAsFactors = FALSE, encoding = "UTF-8", # r-style: keep – the same reader as the workspace
                                 na.strings = c("", "NA")),
           envir = .cache)
  }
  .cache[[name]]
}
.housing   <- function() .read_once("housing", file.path(.data_dir, "housing_emails.csv"))  # r-style: approved
.curve   <- function() .read_once("curve", file.path(.data_dir, "spec_curve.csv"))  # r-style: approved
.options <- function() .read_once("options", file.path(.data_dir, "menu_options.csv"))  # r-style: approved


# ---- Pages of the course site ----------------------------------------------------
.pages <- c(
  "background.qmd"                = "Background",
  "menu.qmd"                      = "Specification menu",
  "menu.qmd#map"                  = "Decision map",
  "curve.qmd"                     = "Specification curve",
  "companion/experiments.qmd"     = "Audit experiments",
  "companion/binary-outcomes.qmd" = "Binary outcomes",
  "companion/dags.qmd"            = "Causal graphs and conditioning",
  "companion/multiverse.qmd"      = "The multiverse and its critics")
.page_ref <- function(path) {  # r-style: approved
  title <- if (path %in% names(.pages)) .pages[[path]] else path
  sprintf("%s, %s/%s", title, .course_url, sub(".qmd", ".html", path, fixed = TRUE))
}
.or_list <- function(x) {  # r-style: approved
  q <- paste0("\"", x, "\"")
  if (length(q) == 1) q else paste(paste(q[-length(q)], collapse = ", "), "or", q[length(q)])
}


# ---- Validation ------------------------------------------------------------------
# Two entry points into the same rules. .validate() takes a named list, which
# is how try_spec() supplies its arguments; .check_choices() reads the eleven
# my_* choices of the preregistration block. An option that is not on the
# curve stops with the reason from menu_options.csv, the page of the course
# site that teaches it, and the options that stay on the curve.
.on_menu <- function(axis, v) is.character(v) && length(v) == 1 && !is.na(v) && v %in% .menu[[axis]]  # r-style: approved

.refuse <- function(axis, v, as_args) {  # r-style: approved
  shown <- if (as_args) axis else paste0("my_", axis)
  keep  <- .menu[[axis]]
  map   <- paste0("  Every decision and its options: ", .page_ref("menu.qmd#map"))
  if (!is.character(v) || length(v) != 1 || is.na(v))
    stop(sprintf("%s needs one option in quotes, for example %s = \"%s\".", shown, shown, keep[1]),
         call. = FALSE)
  opts <- .options()
  row  <- dplyr::filter(opts, .data$axis == .env$axis, .data$option == .env$v)
  off  <- dplyr::filter(opts, .data$axis == .env$axis, !.data$on_curve)$option
  msg <- if (nrow(row) == 1) c(
    sprintf("%s = \"%s\" (%s) is not on the curve of %d specifications, so it has no result here.",
            shown, v, row$label, nrow(.curve())),
    paste0("  Why: ", row$reason),
    paste0("  Where it is taught: ", .page_ref(row$taught_on)),
    map,
    sprintf("  To stay on the curve, choose %s = %s.", shown, .or_list(keep))
  ) else c(
    sprintf("%s = \"%s\" is not an option on the menu.", shown, v),
    sprintf("  On the curve: %s.", paste(keep, collapse = " | ")),
    if (length(off) > 0)
      sprintf("  Off the curve, refused with the reason why: %s.", paste(off, collapse = " | ")),
    map
  )
  stop(paste(msg, collapse = "\n"), call. = FALSE)
}

.validate <- function(ch, as_args = FALSE) {  # r-style: approved
  bad <- purrr::discard(names(.menu), \(a) .on_menu(a, ch[[a]]))
  if (length(bad) > 0) .refuse(bad[1], ch[[bad[1]]], as_args)
  ch[names(.menu)]
}

# The choices are looked up from the frame of this function outwards, which
# reaches the session in which the preregistration block was run.
.check_choices <- function() {  # r-style: approved
  need <- paste0("my_", names(.menu))
  ch <- mget(need, envir = environment(), inherits = TRUE, ifnotfound = list(NULL))
  missing <- need[purrr::map_lgl(ch, is.null)]
  if (length(missing) > 0)
    stop("Not declared yet: ", paste(missing, collapse = ", "),
         ". Fill in every choice in the preregistration block and run it first.", call. = FALSE)
  .validate(stats::setNames(ch, names(.menu)))
}


# ---- The live fit ----------------------------------------------------------------
# fit_spec() on the five decisions that vary on the curve, with the 95%
# interval of the estimate that it returns (a t interval from parameters for
# the linear model, a normal interval from marginaleffects for the average
# marginal effect of the logit) and the place of the result among the 64. The
# fit is checked against its row of data/spec_curve.csv; a difference means
# that the page loaded an incomplete file.
.result <- function(ch) {  # r-style: approved
  fit <- fit_spec(.housing(), ch$comparison, ch$population, ch$uncoded, ch$model, ch$adjust) |>
    as.list()
  curve <- .curve()
  stored <- dplyr::filter(curve, .data$comparison == ch$comparison, .data$population == ch$population,
                          .data$uncoded == ch$uncoded, .data$model == ch$model,
                          .data$adjust == ch$adjust)
  if (nrow(stored) != 1) {
    warning("This specification has no row in data/spec_curve.csv; reload the page.",
            call. = FALSE)
  } else if (abs(fit$b_pp - stored$b_pp) > 1e-6 || abs(fit$stat - stored$stat) > 1e-6) {
    warning(sprintf("The live fit (%.4f points, %s = %.4f) differs from the curve that this page loaded (%.4f points, %s = %.4f). Reload the page.",
                    fit$b_pp, fit$stat_type, fit$stat, stored$b_pp, fit$stat_type, stored$stat),
            call. = FALSE)
  }
  c(fit, list(further = sum(curve$b_pp < fit$b_pp - 1e-9), n_curve = nrow(curve)))
}


# ---- The printout ----------------------------------------------------------------
.comparison_label <- function(comparison)  # r-style: approved
  c(white = "white names", nonhispanic = "white and Black names")[[comparison]]

.fmt_p <- function(p) sprintf("= %s", format(signif(p, 2), scientific = FALSE))  # r-style: approved

.class_line <- function(res) {  # r-style: approved
  below <- res$b_pp < 0
  sig   <- res$p < 0.05
  if (below && sig) "below zero and significant at 5%, in the direction of the claim"
  else if (below) "below zero, but not significant at 5%"
  else if (sig) "above zero and significant at 5%, against the direction of the claim"
  else "above zero and not significant at 5%"
}

.print_result <- function(ch, res, lead = NULL) {  # r-style: approved
  unit <- if (ch$population == "all") "delivered emails" else "replies"
  test <- if (res$stat_type == "t") c(
    sprintf("  Test: t = %.2f on %d df, p %s (linear probability model, HC2 standard errors)",
            res$stat, round(res$df), .fmt_p(res$p))
  ) else c(
    sprintf("  Test: z = %.2f, p %s (logistic regression; the difference is its average marginal effect)",
            res$stat, .fmt_p(res$p)),
    sprintf("        logit coefficient %.3f, standard error %.3f", res$coef, res$coef_se)
  )
  writeLines(c(
    lead,
    paste0("  ", spec_line(ch$comparison, ch$population, ch$uncoded, ch$model, ch$adjust)),
    sprintf("  Greeted by name: Hispanic names %.1f%% of %d %s, %s %.1f%% of %d",
            res$rate_hisp, res$n_hisp, unit, .comparison_label(ch$comparison), res$rate_comp,
            res$n_comp),
    sprintf("  Difference: %.2f percentage points, 95%% interval %.2f to %.2f",
            res$b_pp, res$ci_low, res$ci_high),
    test,
    sprintf("  n = %d %s, partial r = %.3f (the conversion rule of the robustness study)", res$n, unit, res$r),
    paste0("  Verdict: ", .class_line(res)),
    sprintf("  On the curve: %d of the %d specifications have an estimate further below zero",
            res$further, res$n_curve)))
  invisible(res)
}


# ---- Task 4: the exploratory helpers -----------------------------------------------
.tried <- new.env(parent = emptyenv())
assign("log", NULL, envir = .tried)
assign("last", NULL, envir = .tried)

# The first five arguments are the decisions on which the curve keeps more
# than one option; the other six are fixed on the curve, and asking for any
# other option of theirs prints the reason why it is not on the curve.
try_spec <- function(comparison = "white", population = "replies", uncoded = "drop",  # r-style: approved
                     model = "lpm", adjust = "none", outcome = "named", names = "both",
                     officials = "any", bounced = "exclude", inference = "model", scale = "pp") {
  ch <- .validate(list(outcome = outcome, comparison = comparison, population = population,
                       names = names, officials = officials, uncoded = uncoded,
                       bounced = bounced, model = model, adjust = adjust,
                       inference = inference, scale = scale), as_args = TRUE)
  res <- .result(ch)
  .print_result(ch, res, lead = "")
  row <- data.frame(ch, b_pp = res$b_pp, ci_low = res$ci_low, ci_high = res$ci_high,  # r-style: keep – data.frame() spreads the list of choices into columns
                    stat_type = res$stat_type, stat = res$stat, p = res$p, n = res$n,
                    stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  assign("log", dplyr::bind_rows(.tried$log, row), envir = .tried)
  assign("last", list(ch = ch, res = res), envir = .tried)
  invisible(row)
}

# The running log of everything try_spec() has fitted. Only the decisions that
# varied are shown; the others are those of the reference specification.
my_experiments <- function() {  # r-style: approved
  d <- .tried$log
  if (is.null(d)) {
    writeLines("Nothing tried yet – call try_spec() at least once.")
    return(invisible(NULL))
  }
  varied <- purrr::keep(names(.menu), \(a) dplyr::n_distinct(d[[a]]) > 1)
  show <- d |>
    dplyr::transmute(dplyr::across(dplyr::all_of(varied)),
                     estimate = round(.data$b_pp, 2),
                     interval = sprintf("%.1f to %.1f", .data$ci_low, .data$ci_high),
                     test = sprintf("%s = %.2f", .data$stat_type, .data$stat),
                     p = signif(.data$p, 2),
                     n = .data$n)
  writeLines(sprintf("Specifications you have tried (%d), estimates in percentage points:\n", nrow(d)))
  # wide enough for all five varied decisions on one line
  old_width <- options(width = max(getOption("width"), 120))
  on.exit(options(old_width))
  print(show, row.names = FALSE)
  writeLines(sprintf("\nEstimates from %.2f to %.2f points  |  below zero and significant at 5%%: %d of %d",
                     min(d$b_pp), max(d$b_pp), sum(d$b_pp < 0 & d$p < 0.05), nrow(d)))
  invisible(show)
}

# prereg() prints the block and returns it, so that run_spec() can check that
# the block has not changed since.
prereg <- function() {  # r-style: approved
  ch <- .check_choices()
  rows <- .options() |>
    dplyr::filter(paste(.data$axis, .data$option) %in% paste(names(ch), unlist(ch))) |>
    dplyr::arrange(match(.data$axis, names(.menu))) |>
    dplyr::mutate(line = sprintf("    %-31s : %-12s (%s)", .data$decision, .data$option, .data$label))
  block <- purrr::imap(.level_titles, \(title, lv) c(paste0("  ", title), rows$line[rows$level == lv])) |>
    unlist(use.names = FALSE)
  ph <- stats::setNames(rows$phrase, rows$axis)
  statement <- c(
    sprintf("%s%s, %s, %s, the difference in the share that drew %s between Hispanic names and %s (%s, %s).",
            toupper(substr(ph[["population"]], 1, 1)), substring(ph[["population"]], 2),
            ph[["names"]], ph[["officials"]], ph[["outcome"]], ph[["comparison"]],
            ph[["uncoded"]], ph[["bounced"]]),
    sprintf("Estimated with %s, %s, tested by %s and reported %s.",
            ph[["model"]], ph[["adjust"]], ph[["inference"]], ph[["scale"]]))
  writeLines(c(
    "DECLARED – your preregistered specification, fixed before it is fitted:",
    "",
    block,
    "",
    "  The estimand statement",
    strwrap(statement, width = 78, indent = 4, exdent = 4),
    "",
    "run_spec() and report_result() read these choices from here. Rendered into",
    "your report, this block is your preregistration, and it sits above the",
    "cells that fit and submit this specification."))
  invisible(structure(list(choices = ch), class = "housing_prereg"))
}

.new_tag <- function() {  # r-style: approved
  had_seed <- exists(".Random.seed", envir = globalenv(), inherits = FALSE)

  on.exit(if (had_seed) assign(".Random.seed", old_seed, envir = globalenv())

# A nickname reduced to lower-case ASCII letters, digits and single hyphens,
# at most 24 characters – the only form that the class chart parses.
.clean_tag <- function(x) {  # r-style: approved
  # iconv on Windows turns these into "?": the Romanian comma-below letters and the eszett
  x <- gsub("ß", "ss", chartr("ȘșȚț", "SsTt", trimws(as.character(x)[1])))
  ascii <- suppressWarnings(iconv(x, to = "ASCII//TRANSLIT"))
  if (!is.na(ascii)) x <- ascii
  x <- gsub("^-+|-+$", "", gsub("[^a-z0-9]+", "-", tolower(x)))
  x <- gsub("-+$", "", substr(x, 1, 24))
  if (is.na(x) || !nzchar(x))
    stop("A nickname needs at least one letter or digit, for example nickname = \"blue-heron\".",
         call. = FALSE)
  x
}

# The tag of this session: the nickname if one is given, otherwise the tag
# already drawn, otherwise a fresh one. Returns the tag and the one it replaced.
.class_tag <- function(nickname = NULL) {  # r-style: approved
  stored <- .tag_env$tag
  tag <- if (!is.null(nickname)) .clean_tag(nickname) else if (!is.null(stored)) stored else .new_tag()
  assign("tag", tag, envir = .tag_env)
  list(tag = tag, replaced = if (!is.null(stored) && !identical(tag, stored)) stored)
}

             n = as.character(res$n), r = sprintf("%.3f", res$r))
  query <- purrr::imap_chr(.form_entry, \(entry, k)
    paste0(entry, "=", utils::URLencode(value[[k]], reserved = TRUE))) |>
    paste(collapse = "&")
  url <- sprintf("https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/%s/viewform?usp=pp_url&%s", .form_id, query)

  writeLines(c(
    lead,
    "",
    paste("  spec:", spec_label),
    sprintf("  b = %s | se = %s | %s = %s | df = %s | n = %d | r = %s",
            value[["b"]], value[["se"]], res$stat_type, value[["t"]],
            if (nzchar(value[["df"]])) value[["df"]] else "(none, a logit)", res$n, value[["r"]]),
    "  (b and se in percentage points)",
    paste0("  Verdict: ", .class_line(res)),
    "",
    "Open the link below (or copy the URL) – the form opens with every field",
    "pre-filled; just press Send.",
    "",
    url,
    "",
    sprintf("Your marks on the class chart carry the tag %s%s.", tg$tag,
            if (!is.null(tg$replaced)) sprintf(" (it replaces %s)", tg$replaced) else ""),
    sprintf("Look for it on the Class results page, %s/class-results.html.", .course_url),

    sprintf("bring it back with nickname = \"%s\". To choose your own, pass a", tg$tag),
    "nickname rather than your name, because the chart is public."))
  invisible(list(spec = spec_label, tag = tg$tag, b = res$b_pp, se = res$se_pp, statistic = res$stat,

make_dag <- function(..., exposure = "name", outcome = "greeting", latent = "official") {  # r-style: approved
  arrows <- c(...)
  edges <- purrr::map(arrows, \(a) {
    ends <- trimws(strsplit(a, "->", fixed = TRUE)[[1]])

      stop(sprintf("Write each arrow as \"cause -> effect\", for example \"name -> reply\"; \"%s\" is not one.",

  }) |>
    dplyr::bind_rows() |>
    dplyr::distinct()
  structure(list(edges = edges, nodes = unique(c(exposure, outcome, edges$from, edges$to)),
                 exposure = exposure, outcome = outcome, latent = latent,

                             collapse = "; ")),

plot_dag <- function(d) {  # r-style: approved
  parts <- .dag_parts(d)
  nodes <- parts$nodes |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      unplaced = is.na(.data$x),
      x = dplyr::if_else(.data$unplaced, 1.2 * (cumsum(.data$unplaced) - 1), .data$x),
      y = dplyr::if_else(.data$unplaced, -0.9, .data$y),
      half_w = 0.06 + 0.032 * nchar(.data$name),
      role = factor(dplyr::case_when(.data$name %in% parts$exposure ~ "exposure",
                                     .data$name %in% parts$outcome ~ "outcome",
                                     .data$name %in% parts$latent ~ "unobserved",
                                     .default = "observed"),
                    levels = c("exposure", "outcome", "observed", "unobserved")))
  # how far along a unit vector (ux, uy) the edge of a box of half-width w lies
  to_edge <- \(ux, uy, w) pmin(w / pmax(abs(ux), 1e-9), 0.15 / pmax(abs(uy), 1e-9))  # r-style: approved
  tails <- dplyr::select(nodes, from = "name", x0 = "x", y0 = "y", w0 = "half_w")
  heads <- dplyr::select(nodes, to = "name", x1 = "x", y1 = "y", w1 = "half_w")
  arrows <- parts$edges |>
    dplyr::inner_join(tails, by = "from") |>
    dplyr::inner_join(heads, by = "to") |>
    dplyr::mutate(len = sqrt((.data$x1 - .data$x0)^2 + (.data$y1 - .data$y0)^2),
                  ux = (.data$x1 - .data$x0) / .data$len,
                  uy = (.data$y1 - .data$y0) / .data$len,
                  s0 = to_edge(.data$ux, .data$uy, .data$w0),
                  s1 = to_edge(.data$ux, .data$uy, .data$w1) + 0.04,
                  x = .data$x0 + .data$s0 * .data$ux, y = .data$y0 + .data$s0 * .data$uy,
                  xend = .data$x1 - .data$s1 * .data$ux, yend = .data$y1 - .data$s1 * .data$uy)

  # the boxes, coloured by role; tinyplot has no type for arrows, so they go
  # on the same canvas through graphics::arrows(); then the names, white on
  # the coloured boxes and dark on the pale one
  tinyplot::tinyplot(xmin = nodes$x - 0.8 * nodes$half_w, xmax = nodes$x + 0.8 * nodes$half_w,
                     ymin = nodes$y - 0.1, ymax = nodes$y + 0.1, by = nodes$role, type = "rect",
                     palette = c("#1b6ca8", "#d1495b", "grey45", "grey88"), fill = "by",
                     legend = list("bottom!", title = NULL), axes = FALSE, frame.plot = FALSE,
                     xlab = NA, ylab = NA,
                     xlim = range(nodes$x) + c(-0.45, 0.45), ylim = range(nodes$y) + c(-0.3, 0.3),
                     grid = FALSE, theme = "minimal")
  graphics::arrows(arrows$x, arrows$y, arrows$xend, arrows$yend,
                   length = 0.1, angle = 20, col = "grey40", lwd = 1.5)
  tinyplot::tinyplot(x = nodes$x, y = nodes$y, by = nodes$role,
                     type = tinyplot::type_text(labels = nodes$name, font = 2),
                     palette = c("white", "white", "white", "grey25"), cex = 0.85, add = TRUE)
}

## What social science is for {#what-are-we-doing-when-we-do-social-science}

:::: {.none}
::: {.fragment}
Making **claims about the world** that could turn out to be wrong – and saying how we would know.
:::

::: {.fragment}
A claim is offered to others so that they can **check it, use it, argue with it, build on it**.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Science depends on that handover, and everything that follows is about whether it works.
:::
::::

::: notes
Start with the obvious question that nobody asks out loud: what are we actually doing when we do social science? We are making claims about the world – claims that could turn out to be wrong, and that come with some statement of how we would find out. And you publish a claim so that other people can check it, use it, argue with it, and build on top of it. The whole enterprise depends on that handover, and a finding that nobody else can examine remains an assertion. So when we ask whether social science is in trouble, the question is quite specific. Does the handover work, and can someone else pick your finding up and do anything with it?
:::

## False positives and forking paths {#three-arguments-that-made-people-nervous .smaller}

::: {.small}
- **The theory, 2005.** With small studies, small true effects, flexible designs and many teams chasing the same question, most published findings in a field can be false with nobody breaking any rules [@Ioannidis2005WhyMostPublished]
- **The demonstration, 2011.** Give researchers only the flexibility they legitimately have – which cases to drop, which covariates to keep, when to stop collecting – and a **false-positive rate of 5% becomes over 60%** [@SimmonsEtAl2011FalsePositivePsychology]
- **The subtlety, 2014.** You do not need many tests. In a **garden of forking paths**, a single test *chosen after looking at the data* already has the wrong p-value [@GelmanLoken2014StatisticalCrisisScience]
:::

::: notes
Three arguments made people nervous, and I take them in order of how uncomfortable they are. Ioannidis in 2005 made the theoretical case: put together small studies, small true effects, flexible designs and lots of teams chasing the same question, and you can show that most published findings in a field will be false without anybody breaking a single rule. Then Simmons, Nelson and Simonsohn demonstrated it in practice – give researchers only the flexibility they legitimately have, and you can push a five per cent false-positive rate above sixty. They proved it by 'showing', with real participants and real statistics, that listening to a Beatles song makes you younger. And Gelman and Loken added the subtlety that I find hardest to shake: you do not have to run many tests for this to bite. If the one test you ran was chosen after you looked at the data, its p-value is already wrong.
:::

## Evidence from replications and many-analysts studies {#and-then-people-counted .smaller}

::: {.small}
- **100 psychology studies**, replicated with high power and the original materials: **97%** of the originals were significant, **36%** of the replications were, and effect sizes roughly **halved** [@OpenScienceCollaboration2015EstimatingReproducibilityPsychological]
- **161 researchers, 73 teams, one hypothesis** on immigration and support for social policy: **1,253** models, and no convergence on either sign or significance [@BreznauEtAl2022ObservingManyResearchers]
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Different fields and different designs. In the first, **most findings were not significant again in new samples**; in the second, **the result depended on who ran the analysis.**
:::

::: notes
And then people stopped arguing and counted. The Open Science Collaboration took a hundred psychology studies and replicated them properly – high power, original materials, the original authors consulted where possible. Ninety-seven per cent of the original studies had reported a significant result. Thirty-six per cent of the replications did, and the effect sizes came back at about half the original size. That is the study that made 'replication crisis' a phrase outside methodology seminars. The second one is closest to home, because it is ours: seventy-three teams, their members mostly sociologists and political scientists, one hypothesis about immigration and support for social policy, more than twelve hundred models between them, and no agreement on the sign, let alone the significance. Different fields and different designs. In the first, most findings were not significant again when the studies were rerun on new samples; in the second, the finding depended on who did the analysis.
:::

## Incentives and questionable research practices {#it-is-not-mostly-fraud .smaller}

::: {.small}
Fraud exists, but it is rare. The mechanism behind these results is **ordinary and structural**:

- Journals reward novel, clean, significant results – so that is what gets written up
- Every analysis contains dozens of small defensible choices, and the analyst makes them while looking at the data
- Nobody publishes the twelve specifications that did not work; the reader sees one
- Data and code are usually not available, so nobody can check any of it
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Ask researchers anonymously, with an incentive to answer truthfully, and a **majority admit** to at least one of these ordinary practices [@JohnEtAl2012MeasuringPrevalenceQuestionable]
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
None of these steps requires a dishonest person, so the problem cannot be fixed by hiring better people.
:::

::: notes
This is not mostly a story about fraud, and I want to be emphatic about that. Fraud exists and it is spectacular when it surfaces, but it is rare and it is not what these numbers are measuring. The mechanism is ordinary and it is structural. Journals want novel, clean, significant results, so that is what gets submitted. Every analysis contains dozens of small, individually defensible choices, and the analyst makes them while looking at the data, because how else would you make them. Nobody writes up the twelve specifications that did not work, so the reader sees one path through a garden with hundreds. And in most cases neither the data nor the code are available, so nobody can check any of it. John, Loewenstein and Prelec went and asked researchers directly, anonymously, with a mechanism designed to make truthful answers worth giving – and a majority admitted to at least one of these practices. Not one of those steps requires a bad actor, and that is why the problem is hard: you cannot solve it by hiring better people. [pause] So suppose you did hire the best people you could find, gave them all the same data and the same question, and watched what they did.
:::

## Repeatability and credibility {#credibility-is-not-truth}

::: {.scaled style="--fs: 0.9; --lh: 1.15"}
"**Repeatability** is used when referring to reproducibility, robustness, and replicability as a constellation of concepts intended to assess whether answers to scientific questions are unchanged when different steps of the research process are repeated."

**Credibility** and **trustworthiness** refer to the confidence one can have in research findings. Because scientific knowledge claims are tentative, they are *not* synonymous with truth.

"For example, credibility is advanced by addressing potential competing interests in the conducting and reporting of research, by taking existing knowledge into account, by using methods that have been validated, by controlling for biases in the research context, by pursuing precise and reliable evidence, and by calibrating the strength of the claims to the uncertainty of the evidence."
:::

::: {.src}
@NosekEtAl2025BriefGlossaryTerms [p. 2]
:::

::: notes
The glossary on this slide is worth reading slowly, because it separates two things we routinely run together. Repeatability is the umbrella: reproducibility, robustness and replicability as a family, all asking whether the answer survives repeating some step of the process. Credibility and trustworthiness are about how much confidence a finding deserves – and note the sentence in the middle. Because scientific claims are tentative, credibility is not the same as truth. A credible finding can be wrong. What credibility is built from is the list at the bottom: declared interests, validated methods, precise evidence, and claims calibrated to the uncertainty behind them. That last one is the one we will keep coming back to.
:::

## Open research: the practices {.smaller}

::: {.small}
| Practice | What it makes possible |
|---|---|
| **Open data** | Someone else can re-analyse your evidence |
| **Open code** | Someone else can rerun your exact analysis |
| **Open materials** | Someone else can run your study again |
| **Open access** | Someone else can read the claim in the first place |
| **Preregistration** | A dated record of the analysis plan, filed in a registry before the results exist |
| **Registered reports** | Peer review of the plan, with publication decided before results |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Each one removes a specific obstacle, and none of them guards against every problem. The programme, set out at length: [@MunafoEtAl2017ManifestoReproducibleScience]
:::

::: notes
Each of those reviewers needed something from you before they could start – your code, your data, your materials. Open research is a list of practices that supply those things and more, each of which removes a specific, identifiable obstacle. Open data means someone else can re-analyse your evidence rather than taking your word for it. Open code means they can rerun your exact analysis. Open materials means they can run the study again in a new sample. Open access means they can read the thing at all, which sounds trivial until you try to get a paper from outside a wealthy university. Preregistration produces a dated record of the analysis plan, filed in a registry before the results exist. And registered reports go further: the plan is peer-reviewed and the publication decision is made before anyone sees a result, which removes the incentive to find something. Each removes one obstacle, and none of them guards against every problem. Whether published findings hold up when somebody does check them has now been measured on a large scale.
:::

## SCORE in brief {#score-in-brief .smaller}

::: {.fs-80}
| Repetition | The study | What came back |
|:-----|:-----|:-----|
| **Reproduction** – same data, same analysis | 600 papers from 62 journals, 2009–2018 [@MiskeEtAl2026InvestigatingReproducibilitySocial] | Of the 143 that could be assessed, **53.6%** reproduced precisely and **73.5%** at least approximately; counting the papers that nobody could check, about **18%** |
| **Robustness** – same data, other analyses | The robustness study: 100 studies, at least 5 analysts each [Multi100\; @AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness] | **74%** of reanalyses reached the same conclusion; **34%** came within ±0.05 *d* of the original effect size |
| **Replication** – new data | 274 claims, independent data [@TynerEtAl2026InvestigatingReplicabilitySocial] | **55.1%** significant again; the median effect size fell from *r* = 0.25 to 0.10 |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Measured on the same body of papers, the three are **essentially uncorrelated**: knowing how a finding fared on one tells you almost nothing about the others.
:::

::: notes
SCORE, a programme funded by the research agency of the US Department of Defense, took a sample of social-science papers and put their central claims through each of the three repetitions on the grid. Reproduction first: of six hundred papers, the authors supplied data for about a quarter, and of the hundred and forty-three that could be assessed, about half reproduced precisely and three quarters approximately. Count the papers that nobody could check, and the rate is about eighteen per cent. Robustness was the subject of the robustness study, known as Multi100, where at least five analysts reanalysed each claim: three quarters reached the same conclusion, but only a third came close to the original effect size. Replication on new data: fifty-five per cent significant again, with effect sizes more than halved. [advance] And the three barely predict one another, so for any one paper you have to ask which of the three it passed.
:::

## What an analyst of the robustness study received {#what-an-analyst-received .smaller}

::: {.small}
- A **published paper**, in full and not blinded, so the original estimates were in view
- Its **central claim**, in one sentence, usually taken from the abstract
- The **data**, or directions for fetching them
- No instructions on method – any analysis you can defend
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
And two things that no analyst was told: **who the other analysts were**, and **what they were finding**.
:::

::: {.src}
@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness; preregistration of the robustness study, osf.io/4ev9t, pp. 4–5.
:::

::: notes
The robustness study of SCORE, known as Multi100, handed a hundred published studies to at least five independent analysts each, and I was one of those analysts, on a different paper from the one we work on today. Let me describe what that was like from the inside, because it shapes how you read the results. What arrived was the published paper, the whole thing and not blinded, so the original estimates were in view, and if anything that pulls you towards the original answer. With it came the central claim of the paper in a single sentence, usually taken from the abstract, and the data or directions for fetching them. What did not arrive was any instruction on method: analyse it however you can defend. And two things stayed hidden throughout, who the other analysts were and what any of them were finding. The isolation was part of the design, because it is what makes the spread at the end mean something.
:::

## The two tasks of the robustness study {#two-tasks-months-apart .smaller}

::: {.small}
**Task 1 – free reanalysis.** Reanalyse the claim however you see fit, then record one conclusion: evidence for the claim, evidence for the opposite, no evidence either way, or evidence for the null hypothesis.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
**Task 2 – constrained reanalysis.** Once Task 1 was in, instructions arrived: report a single main result from the family of *z*, *t*, *F* or $\chi^2$ tests (or an alternative or non-parametric version), with an instruction for each claim that fixed one or two details of the analysis.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Task 1 measures whether analysts reach the same verdict. Task 2 makes their *numbers* comparable, since five answers to five different questions cannot be averaged.
:::

::: notes
The study ran in two stages, and the distinction matters for everything that follows. Task one was complete freedom: reanalyse the claim however you see fit, and record one categorical conclusion out of four, evidence for the claim, evidence for the opposite, no evidence either way, or evidence for the null hypothesis. [advance] Once that was submitted, task two arrived. It asked for a single main result in the form of a test statistic, and it came with a short instruction for each claim that pinned down one or two details of the analysis. [advance] The order matters because the two tasks measure different things. Task one asks whether independent analysts reach the same verdict. Task two asks whether they produce the same number, and that question can only be asked once everyone is answering roughly the same question, which is what the instructions were for. We will read the instruction for our own claim later.
:::

## Results on a common scale {#how-a-hundred-studies-become-one-number .smaller}

::: {.small}
- Every analyst reports a test statistic in whatever form the model produces – **t**, **z**, **F**, $\chi^2$ – with its degrees of freedom or its sample size
- Each is converted to a **partial correlation** *r* and a standardised **Cohen's *d***, so that a regression fitted in Stata and a test computed in R can be read on one axis
- A **peer panel** judges whether each pipeline is an appropriate analysis of the claim
- Only then can you ask how far apart several defensible answers are
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Standardising makes the comparison possible, but it assumes that the analysts are estimating **the same quantity**, and that the numbers fed into each conversion count the units that carry the evidence. Hold both thoughts.
:::

::: notes
Even with the question pinned down, the answers arrive in different forms. Everyone reports the test statistic that their model happens to produce, a t, a z, an F or a chi-square, with its degrees of freedom or its sample size. The robustness study converted those onto a common scale, a partial correlation and a standardised difference, so that a regression fitted in Stata and a test computed in R could be placed on the same axis. Alongside that, a peer panel judged whether each pipeline was an appropriate analysis of the claim at all, so the spread that comes out of the study is a spread among analyses that passed review. [advance] Putting several numbers on one axis takes two things for granted. One is that they estimate the same quantity, and a good deal of what follows is about what happens when they do not. The other is that each conversion counts the units that actually carry the evidence.
:::

First, the theoretical estimand: a unit-specific quantity and a target population, stated in plain words, before any model exists. Second, the empirical estimand, which is what in the observable data corresponds to that quantity – and making that link forces your identification assumptions into the open, which is the job of the causal graph. ## Confounders, mediators and colliders {#dag-crash-course-three-roles .smaller}


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](day_files/figure-revealjs/mini-dags-1.png){width=912}
:::
:::


::: {.src}
X = predictor, Y = outcome. **Green** = the causal effect you want; **coloured** = the path you must reason about.
:::

::: notes
The causal graph is the second of those three steps, and these three small graphs cover all the graph theory that the tasks need. In every panel the green arrow is the same thing, the effect of X on Y that you are actually after. What changes is the coloured structure around it. A confounder is a common cause of your predictor and your outcome – that red fork is a back-door path, and if you leave it open you are biased, so you adjust to close it. A mediator lies on the causal path between them. The amber path is real and part of the total effect, so if the total effect is what you want you do not adjust for it, or you remove part of the very thing you are measuring. And a collider is caused by both sides – those edges are harmless until you condition on the collider, which opens a spurious path that was not there before. So the rulebook is short: adjust confounders, leave mediators alone for total effects, and never condition on a collider. The next four slides add a little depth to those three rules before you use them.
:::

## Reading a DAG: open and closed paths {.smaller}


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](day_files/figure-revealjs/backdoor-paths-1.png){width=912}
:::
:::


::: {.small}
Association flows along **every open path**, not only along the causal arrow. A fork or a chain is open until you adjust for the variable in its middle. A collider is the reverse: shut by default, and opened when you adjust for it.

- **Back-door criterion**: close every path that enters X from behind, keep the causal X → Y path open
- Only an adjustment set that does this supports a causal reading
:::

::: {.src}
@HernanRobins2020CausalInferenceWhat; @Huntington-Klein2021EffectIntroductionResearch.
:::

::: notes
A DAG is read through its paths. Association flows along every open path between X and Y, not only down the causal arrow. So the job is to work out which paths are open and shut the ones you do not want. Two rules do all the work. A path through a fork or a chain is open, and you close it by adjusting the variable in the middle – that is the red back-door fork on the left. A path through a collider is the opposite. It is shut by default, and you open it by adjusting. The back-door criterion puts the two rules together: close every path that sneaks into X from behind, and leave the causal X-to-Y path alone. Only an adjustment set that does that gives you an estimate you are allowed to read as causal.
:::

- **Total** = direct (green) + indirect (amber)
- Adjust for the mediator M → you estimate the **direct** effect only – a *different* estimand

@KeeleEtAl2020CausalInterpretationEstimated; @DAgostinoMcGowanEtAl2024CausalInferenceNot.
:::

::: notes
Suppose M lies between your predictor and your outcome. The total effect is the green arrow plus the amber route through M. The direct effect is just the green arrow. These are different numbers and different questions – and which one you get depends entirely on whether you put M in the model. Drop a mediator in as just another 'control' and you have silently switched to the direct effect without telling anyone, including yourself. This is why 'control for everything' is bad advice. And it has a famous corollary, the Table 2 fallacy. When you print a regression table, usually only one coefficient has a clean causal reading. The coefficients on the control variables are not little causal effects of their own.

- **Reverse causation & feedback** – in a panel, which follows the same units over time, today's outcome can move tomorrow's predictor; adjusting for the stable traits of each unit does **not** remove that feedback, and a randomised experiment avoids it by design
:::

::: {.src}
@GriffithEtAl2020ColliderBiasUndermines; @ColeEtAl2010IllustratingBiasDue; @LeszczenskyWolbring2022HowDealReverse.
:::

::: notes
Two last ways in which a relationship can be spurious. The first is selection, or collider bias. If you condition on – or merely sample on – something that both your variables cause, you manufacture a correlation out of nothing. A lot of the early COVID risk-factor findings were of this kind, drawn from people who had been tested, which is a selected group. Hold on to this one, because it comes back in our own case study in a form that is easy to miss. The second is reverse causation and feedback. In a panel, which follows the same people or places over time, today's outcome can feed tomorrow's predictor, and adjusting for the stable differences between units does not, on its own, fix a confounder that changes over time or a feedback loop. A randomised experiment escapes this second problem by design, because nothing that happens later can change who received which treatment.
:::

::: {.small}
| Emails counted | Hispanic names | White names | Difference |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| Coded replies (n = 362) | 41.2% | 61.1% | −19.97 points |

## The continuity correction {#the-continuity-correction .smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.small}
8PTRZ, the replies with a code:

| | Not greeted by name | Greeted by name |
|:--|--:|--:|
| Hispanic names | 110 | 77 |
| All other names | 154 | 217 |
:::
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{.r}
chisq.test(tab_8ptrz)
chisq.test(tab_8ptrz, correct = FALSE)
```

::: {.small}
With the correction, $\chi^2$ = **14.265**; without it, $\chi^2$ = **14.952**.
:::
:::
::::

::: {.fragment .small}
For a two-by-two table, `chisq.test()` and `prop.test()` both apply the **continuity correction** unless told otherwise: it shrinks each gap between an observed and an expected count by half a count before squaring. 8PTRZ and 25N5D kept the default, and so did you. For 25N5D the test gives 13.683 with it and 14.334 without it.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
A reproduction depends on the **defaults and the codings of the software** as well as on the data and the model. The *z* of EWFMI is positive because its model takes the Hispanic names as the base group.
:::

::: notes
Here is the table of 8PTRZ: replies to Hispanic names and to all other names, greeted by name or not. The printout of chisq dot test has a first line that most people skip: Pearson's chi-square test with Yates' continuity correction. [advance] For a two-by-two table, R applies that correction by default, in chisq dot test and in prop dot test alike. It shrinks each gap between an observed and an expected count by half a count before squaring, which makes the test a little more cautious. Turn it off and 8PTRZ gets fourteen point nine five, 25N5D fourteen point three three. Both analysts kept the default, you kept the default, and that is why your values match the record to the third decimal. [advance] The coding matters in the same way: EWFMI took the Hispanic names as the base group, so its z is positive. A script that relies on a default is reproducible only for as long as that default stays put.
:::

## Standard errors for a 0/1 outcome {#standard-errors-for-a-binary-outcome .smaller .deepdive run="methods"}

::: {.small}
- The variance of a 0/1 outcome is *p*(1 − *p*), so it differs between groups whose shares differ
- **Conventional** standard errors assume one common variance; **HC2** errors, one of the 'heteroskedasticity-consistent' or 'robust' errors, let each group keep its own
- For a comparison of two groups, the HC2 error is, to within a hair, the standard error of a difference between two independent proportions
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
On the reference comparison the two agree: HC2 **5.16** points, conventional **5.17**. With covariates or very unequal groups they part, which is why the curve uses HC2 throughout.
:::

::: notes
A word on the standard errors, because the menu lists them. When the outcome is zero or one, its variance is the share times one minus the share, so two groups with different shares have different variances. Conventional regression errors assume one common variance for everybody, which a linear probability model breaks by construction. HC2 errors, one member of the family that people call robust errors, let each group keep its own variance, and for a simple comparison of two groups they come out, to within a hair, as the textbook standard error of a difference between two proportions. [advance] On our reference comparison the two kinds agree to within two hundredths of a point, because the groups are similar in size and in share. With covariates, or with groups of very different sizes, they can part, so the curve uses HC2 everywhere.
:::

## Where the idea comes from {.smaller .deepdive run="methods"}

::: {.skiplink}
[Multiverse background, 2 slides – skip to the curve →](#the-curve-of-the-claim)
:::

::: {.small}
- **Multiverse analysis** [@SteegenEtAl2016IncreasingTransparencyMultiverse] – developed for *data-processing* choices: how you code, exclude and combine. Report the whole set of datasets that your choices could have produced
- **Specification curve analysis** [@SimonsohnEtAl2020SpecificationCurveAnalysis] – the same move for *model* choices, plus a visual grammar: estimates on top, the choices that produced each one underneath
- **The vibration of effects** – the same idea, arrived at independently in epidemiology
- **The book-length treatment** [@YoungCumberworth2025MultiverseAnalysisComputational] – computational recipes at scale
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Under all these names the proposal is the same: **stop treating your analytical choices as invisible, and enumerate them.**
:::

::: notes
A brief history, because the vocabulary is a mess and knowing which word came from where helps. Multiverse analysis is Steegen and colleagues in 2016, and it grew out of data-processing choices specifically – how you code a variable, which cases you exclude, how you combine items – with the proposal that you report the whole set of datasets that your choices could have produced. Specification curve analysis is Simonsohn, Simmons and Nelson, making the same move for model choices and adding a visual grammar: estimates plotted on top, and underneath them a panel showing which choices produced each one. The vibration of effects is the same idea arrived at independently in epidemiology, which suggests that it is a natural response to the problem. And there is now a book-length treatment with computational recipes. Under different names, they all make the same proposal: stop treating your analytical choices as invisible, and enumerate them.
:::

One more lens: power, the probability that a study of a given size detects a gap of a given size. At a white share of sixty-one per cent, the original comparison, with about a hundred and eighty replies a group, detects a twenty-point gap almost every time. ::: notes
This is the lesson of the case study, and of the course. On the original data the claim is hard to dislodge: every justifiable analysis finds the gap, and only its size moves. [advance] But every one of those analyses works on the same thousand emails, the same six names, the same officials in the same week of 2014. A specification curve varies the analysis and holds the sample fixed, so it cannot tell you what a new sample would show. [advance] Robustness to analytic choices on one sample is a different property from replicability. [advance] Why might the two studies differ? The names are one candidate: names that are meant to indicate one group are not all read the same way, and Santiago and Gabriela may also have read as younger. ## Critics of the multiverse {#the-multiverse-has-its-critics .smaller}

::: {.small}
- "Robustness is better assessed with a **few thoughtful models** than with billions of regressions" [@Auspurg2025RobustnessBetterAssessed; answering @GanslmeierVlandas2025EstimatingExtentSources] – only *justified* models targeting the *same estimand* belong in one curve. The curve of this course keeps only the specifications that a review of every option judged justifiable for the claim, and setting each option beside its twins does the job that every critic endorses: it locates where the argument must happen
- "**There is only one correct analysis**" once the question is fully specified [@LakensEtAl2026ThereOnlyOne] – your preregistered specification guards against *cherry-picking*, and their deeper point is that preregistering a choice does not yet make it *justified*, which is what the estimand and DAG work were for

## The one-correct-analysis argument {#there-is-only-one-correct-analysis .smaller}

::: {.small}
The argument from Lakens and colleagues runs in four steps:

- A research question, **fully specified**, implies a quantity to be estimated
- That quantity, together with the design and the assumptions you are willing to make, implies **one analysis** that estimates it
- So a spread of results is not evidence of legitimate diversity. It is evidence that **most of those specifications are wrong** – they estimate something else
- On this reading, showing a wide curve is closer to an admission than to a robustness check
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Take it back to the red cards. Twenty-nine teams modelled one count of red cards as **linear, logistic or Poisson**. Those are claims about how the outcome was generated, and they cannot all be right – so on this argument most of the spread is error.
:::

::: {.src}
@LakensEtAl2026ThereOnlyOne
:::

::: notes
The strongest objection to the multiverse approach comes from Lakens and colleagues, and I want to give it its full force. They argue that a research question, once fully specified, implies a quantity to be estimated. That quantity, together with your design and the assumptions you are prepared to make, implies one analysis that estimates it. From which it follows that a spread of results is evidence that most of those specifications are wrong, because they estimate something other than what you said you wanted, and not evidence of legitimate analytical diversity at all. And on that reading, publishing a wide specification curve is closer to an admission that you never specified your question than to a robustness check. That is an uncomfortable argument and I think it is largely right.
:::

## Two points from the literature {#two-sentences-worth-keeping}

::: {.claimcard}
"the common single-path analyses in social and behavioural research should not be simply assumed to be robust to alternative analyses" [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness]
:::

::: {.claimcard}
A blueprint: precise question → causal reasoning (DAG) → multiverse → sensitivity analysis [@AuspurgBruderl2021HasCredibilitySocial]
:::

::: {.small}

- Justifiability is the criterion – choose with reasons, show the spread

::: notes
The first point comes from the paper on the robustness study: single-path analyses should not simply be assumed robust. A single path can be a good path, and still the reader is owed the space around it, so a report needs the chosen path and the alternatives together. From Auspurg and Brüderl comes the constructive recipe that we followed today: a precise question, explicit assumptions drawn as a graph, a multiverse, and a sensitivity analysis. And keep the two robustness standards apart in your own writing: the same conclusion, which was reached by seventy-four per cent of the reanalyses in the robustness study, and the same number, which only thirty-four per cent came close to. When you claim robustness, say which one you mean.
